subject: SIG follow-up: tenant blast radius, KV cache & process isolation for Dedicated pools
messages:

Subject: SIG follow-up: clarifications around Dedicated tenancy (blast radius, noisy neighbor)

Hi Vivek,

Thanks again for starting the SIG intake earlier this week. Our security team reviewed the initial responses and has a handful of clarifying questions focused on Dedicated GPU tenancy — primarily around blast radius controls and noisy-neighbor mitigation. Sending these as short bullets to make it easy to include in our intake ticket.

1) Do tenant workloads ever share the same GPU process or CUDA context in a Dedicated pool? If so, under what conditions?
2) Is GPU memory ever shared between tenants (e.g., shared pages, persistent caches)?
3) How is the KV/prefix cache scoped? Is there any possibility of cross-tenant cache leakage when tenants run similar prompts?
4) For noisy-neighbor mitigation, what guardrails do you have (cgroups, MIG, strict capping, autoscaling policies)? Any perf telemetry you can share would help.
5) Please attach any network/architecture diagrams and the completed SIG spreadsheet for our archive.

We need a written statement we can include in the procurement packet that says explicitly whether GPU memory/cuda contexts are shared across tenants in Dedicated pools.

Thanks — if you can get this back by EOD Friday (our procurement window), that would keep the review moving.

Evelyn Shaw

Hi Evelyn — thanks for the focused list. I pulled together concise answers below and attached a completed SIG spreadsheet (SIG-responses-answers.xlsx) plus a short network/isolation diagram. High-level summary first: Dedicated GPU pools are tenant-isolated at the process and memory level by default; we do not share CUDA contexts or GPU memory pages across tenant containers in Dedicated.

Answers (short):
1) Do tenant workloads ever share the same GPU process or CUDA context in a Dedicated pool?
   - No. In Dedicated, tenant workloads run in dedicated containerized serving processes (per-tenant process groups) and we do not multiplex multiple tenants into the same process or CUDA context.
2) Is GPU memory ever shared between tenants (e.g., shared pages, persistent caches)?
   - No. CUDA contexts and device allocations are scoped to the tenant process. Memory pages allocated by one tenant's process are not mapped into another tenant's address space.
3) How is the KV/prefix cache scoped? Is there any possibility of cross-tenant cache leakage?
   - Cache keys are namespaced by tenant ID and enforced at the runtime layer. For Dedicated, we run per-tenant cache instances (in-process or per-tenant Redis depending on configuration) — there is no cross-tenant shared in-memory cache.
4) Noisy-neighbor mitigation — guardrails
   - cgroups for CPU/GPU scheduling limits where supported
   - optional NVIDIA MIG partitioning to slice a physical GPU (available on qualifying hardware)
   - strict CUDA memory caps per container + runtime-level admission control for concurrent streams
   - autoscaling and burst pools to absorb sudden load spikes
   - monitoring + automated remediation (evict / throttle offending tenant)
5) Evidence and artifacts
   - Attached: SIG-responses-answers.xlsx, isolation-network-diagram.pdf, kv-cache-lifecycle.png
   - Also linked: detailed SIG record and supporting logs (see links in metadata).

Written statement you can include: "Redwood Inference Dedicated GPU pools provide per-tenant process and memory isolation. We do not share CUDA contexts or GPU memory pages across tenant workloads. Caching is namespaced per-tenant, and we enforce isolation via containerization, runtime-level namespacing, and optional hardware partitioning (NVIDIA MIG)."

I asked Marcus to add a bit more technical detail on cgroups/MIG and the cache lifecycle; his note is below. Please confirm if you need perf traces or specific log excerpts and we can attach exports.

Best,

Evelyn — adding the technical details requested. Short answers first, then supporting notes and references to the attached diagram.

1) Cache eviction and backing store
   - Prefix/KV cache is namespaced by tenant id. In Dedicated mode we default to per-tenant in-process caches for hot prefixes (L1) and a per-tenant Redis instance for warm/longer-lived items (L2) when enabled. L2 stores are provisioned as tenant-bound instances in the Dedicated environment; there is no shared Redis cluster across tenants unless a customer explicitly requests a shared Redis (not the default).
   - Eviction: L1 (in-process) is ephemeral and tied to the serving process. Evicted items are not moved to other tenants. L2 follows standard LRU expiry/persistence rules but is scoped by tenant. There is no mechanism by which an evicted key from tenant A would surface in tenant B.

2) Kernel-level GPU memory sharing
   - On our Dedicated nodes we run tenant containers inside separate userland processes with isolated CUDA contexts. The CUDA driver associates GPU allocations with a process context; the kernel does not map a user allocation across an unrelated process address space. Therefore, physical GPU memory pages allocated by process A are not mapped into process B's address space.
   - Additional hardware-level isolation: on supported GPUs we offer optional NVIDIA MIG partitions which create independent device slices with separate contexts and scheduling.

References / evidence:
   - See isolation-network-diagram.pdf (page 2): shows per-tenant process boundary and L1/L2 cache placement.
   - See kv-cache-lifecycle.png: cache lifecycle and namespace enforcement.
   - We can export a short kernel allocation trace (dmesg + CUDA driver allocation logs) under a non-prod tenant demonstrating per-process allocations if you want concrete log snippets.

If that level of kernel evidence is required for procurement, tell us the exact log window you need and we will produce sanitized excerpts.

—Marcus
